title: I Think I Love My Wife
full_review:
Comedian Chris Rock juggles duties as director, co-writer and star in "I Think I Love My Wife" (Fox), a dubious remake of the 1972 French classic "Chloe in the Afternoon," the last of director Eric Rohmer's "Six Moral Tales."

Rock falls short both behind and in front of the camera where he plays Richard Cooper, a suburban husband struggling to remain faithful to his wife. His film skimps not only on any special insights into marital fidelity but also on pure entertainment value.

Richard lives outside Manhattan where he works as an investment banker. He's got the proverbial itch after seven years of marriage to schoolteacher Brenda (Gina Torres), who shoulders most of the burden of caring for their two young children. In voice-over, he confesses to being primed for adultery because of his wandering eye and a lack of intimacy with Brenda. Couples therapy isn't helping. When an old acquaintance, Nikki (Kerry Washington), shows up at his office wearing a red dress, he's put to the test.

Richard's predicament plays out in repetitive fashion, with few obvious points overlooked. Twice he attends an auto show -- first with Nikki to admire a Porsche and then with Brenda to scout out minivans. Racial issues are raised occasionally though not in relation to the central theme. The women are one-dimensional. Attractive, intelligent Brenda is prone to nagging and Nikki's needy seductress is a gold digger. Every character is objectified and no one is very likable.

Directing oneself is a formidable challenge and Richard's listlessness is the only evidence that Rock tried to tone down his usual persona. The movie's funniest moment comes when Richard revs up the energy level to pick a fight with Brenda over the dinner menu.

A handful of decent topical jokes get lost under a torrent of four-letter words and sex-related gags.

When Richard finally gets himself into a seriously compromising situation, a modicum of suspense is generated about whether he'll do the right thing. Unfortunately, it's not worth sitting through "I Think I Love My Wife" to find out -- even though, ultimately (slight spoiler here), there's a morally sound outcome.

The film contains pervasive rough and sexually explicit language and an instance of profanity, sexual situations and humor, one image of pornography containing rear female nudity, and a brief violent scuffle. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
